query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an fcc matrix, degradation at high temperature in both oxidizing and reducing environments is governed by the selective oxidation of Cr (and to a lesser extent Al) that forms a brittle, poorly adherent Cr-rich oxide scale. In oxidizing gases this scale grows and then spalls under thermal cycling, while in reducing environments the absence of oxygen destabilizes or prevents the formation of a coherent protective scale, leading to internal oxidation and elemental redistribution. These processes induce microstructural embrittlement that eventually triggers catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built, additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an fcc matrix, residual stresses, and characteristic microstructural features from rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: A controlled pre-oxidation surface treatment designed to form a thin, uniform, and adherent Cr2O3 layer prior to high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Expose specimens at elevated temperatures (e.g., 900–1100°C) for prolonged durations (e.g., 500–1000 hours) under both oxidizing conditions (e.g., 1 atm O2 or air) and reducing conditions (e.g., 5 vol% H2 in an inert gas atmosphere).
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and adherence of the surface oxide scale (primarily Cr2O3) that forms during pre-oxidation and its effect on subsequent oxidation/scaling dynamics.
generation.mechanism: Selective element oxidation results in the formation of a protective yet brittle Cr-rich oxide scale. Under thermal cycling or under reducing conditions that inhibit scale stabilization, the scale either spalls or fails to form properly. This leaves the underlying alloy exposed to rapid internal oxidation and microstructural degradation, thus compromising mechanical integrity and leading to catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens that receive the pre-oxidation treatment should develop a more stable and adherent Cr2O3 scale, delaying degradation. Compared to untreated samples, these pre-oxidized specimens are predicted to show reduced oxide scale spallation, fewer microstructural defects (such as internal oxidation or grain boundary degradation), and improved retention of mechanical properties after the high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The as-built, untreated additively manufactured alloy that, when exposed to high temperatures in oxidizing or reducing environments, rapidly forms unstable oxide scales which spall and lead to early catastrophic failure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under sustained exposures above approximately 900°C and at atmospheres where oxygen (or its absence in reducing environments) plays a critical role in oxidation kinetics. It may not hold at lower temperatures or in cases where other degradation mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide formation/spallation and the relative influence of oxidizing versus reducing conditions on scale stability remain uncertain and require further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples: one group receives a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to form a thin, adherent Cr2O3 scale (e.g., via a short exposure to a mild oxidizing environment at a lower temperature), while the control group is left as-built. Expose both sample sets to high temperatures (e.g., 1000°C) for 500 hours under two different gas atmospheres: one set in 1 atm O2 (oxidizing conditions) and another in a reducing gas mixture (5 vol% H2 in an inert gas). After exposure, characterize the oxide scale (using SEM, TEM, XRD for phase identification), assess the level of scale spallation, and determine residual mechanical properties (using tensile or bending tests).
measurements: Oxide scale composition, morphology, and thickness
Extent and frequency of scale spallation or delamination
Residual mechanical strength (e.g., yield strength, ultimate tensile strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale stability (i.e., less spallation, more uniform scale) and mechanical integrity compared to the untreated controls under either oxidizing or reducing conditions, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation and resulting scale instability govern degradation and catastrophic failure is falsified.
